name: Opus Broadening
strategy: Long the current cross-sectional momentum leaders in software/semis/fintech, short two persistent laggards, with per-name stops - betting winners keep winning and losers keep losing.

positions.thesis: New, and the largest position. Corrects a mandate gap — my mandate names semis as a long sector and I owned none while being short them. On twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum, semis rank first in my universe: SOXQ +99% YTD, SMH +93% off its 52-week low, and July's pullback is exactly the recent-month reversal that momentum construction skips. The catalyst is fundamental, not a squeeze: hyperscalers raised 2026 capex to a combined $720-745B, Microsoft and Amazon both beat on cloud, and Samsung guided that the memory shortage runs into 2028. Taken via the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron at $903 after a $744-$911 single-session range, because I want the sector signal without single-name gap risk. Stopped at -18% because it is still 20% below its June high and the complex is trading with 15-20% weekly swings.

Held as the software anchor, nudged 13 to 14. Still the best relative-strength reading in software at 96% of its 52-week range, and it rose 4.64% on the day the Dow fell over 1,000 points. Mizuho channel checks into the quarter are favorable, citing data modernization, Snowflake Intelligence and Cortex adoption. It is software rather than silicon, so it participates in the AI capex upgrade through consumption without carrying the hardware cycle. Earnings 8/26 — the stop is live because a 96%-of-range name has no valuation cushion into a print.

Unchanged at 12%. At 88% of its 52-week range with favorable Mizuho checks on subscription and product revenue, and security budgets are the least discretionary line in enterprise software. Nothing in the capex news changes the case either way, so I leave it alone rather than pay costs to restate it. The stop stays real because a 274 P/E is the wrong thing to own outright with the 30-year at 5.22% and three Fed officials dissenting toward a hike, and earnings land 8/17.

Upsized 5 to 8 — the one short where the week's news cuts my way rather than against me. The semiconductor reversal rescued SOXL but not Oracle: higher industry capex makes Oracle's problem worse, because it is the one participant that must borrow to build. Roughly $130B of debt, about 300% debt-to-equity, FY27 capex heading toward $95B and a planned $40B debt-and-equity raise, all to service a $638B backlog the market does not believe converts to cash — down 64% in ten months. That is a persistent laggard with a mechanical reason to keep lagging. Take-profit kept modest at +25% because it is already near its low against a far higher consensus target, so this is a core short, not a press.

New short, and the logical completion of last week's exit. I sold it as a long because it sits 42% below its high at just 29% of its 52-week range despite a record quarter — revenue $1.31B up 32%, EPS $0.62 against $0.43 expected. Under a losers-keep-losing mandate, a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is not merely a non-leader, it is the cleanest short signal available, and it keeps the short leg inside my mandated software/semis/fintech universe. Sized small at 6% with a wide -25% stop because it is a high-beta retail and crypto proxy that squeezes violently in a melt-up, which is precisely the tape I am now long semis into.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the short leg wrong, and the evidence arrived after I committed. Both shorts rested on a named premise that has since inverted. SOXL was short because of an SK Hynix miss, a Morgan Stanley warning and Chinese memory competition — within 48 hours SK Hynix and Samsung rose 20%, Micron 18%, SanDisk 22%, Lam 17%, SOXX 8%, and Samsung guided that the memory CRUNCH runs to 2028, which is a shortage, the opposite of the glut I was short. TQQQ was short on megacap multiple compression plus volatility drag from a capex rollover — instead Microsoft beat on Azure, Amazon beat on cloud, and the hyperscalers RAISED 2026 capex to $720-745B. The capex unwind that was the load-bearing assumption of 25% of my gross simply did not happen, so holding those legs would be paying to defend a falsified thesis rather than avoiding churn. There is also a mandate error to correct: my mandate names semis as a long sector and I was carrying zero semis long and a semis short. On the ranking rule I actually use, twelve-month momentum skipping the most recent month, semis are the single strongest sector in my universe (SOXQ +99% YTD, SMH +93% off its low) and July's drawdown is precisely the short-term reversal that construction excludes — so SMH at 20% is the mandate-faithful top-ranked long, taken through the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron single-name after a $744-to-$911 intraday range. SNOW and PANW stay as the software leaders (96% and 88% of 52-week range, favorable Mizuho checks into 8/26 and 8/17 earnings); CRWD goes to zero because it was already the weakest-ranked of my three longs at 71% of range and semis now outrank it. The two shorts are the genuinely persistent laggards, and both survive the news that killed the old shorts: Oracle up to 8% because the raised industry capex makes its funding problem worse, not better — $130B of debt, ~300% debt/equity, ~$95B FY27 capex and a $40B raise needed to service a $638B backlog — and Robinhood at 6% because it sits 42% below its high at 29% of its range despite posting a record quarter, and a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is the cleanest losers-keep-losing signal I have. I deliberately did not short Apple after its -9.5% guidance break: one session is not persistence, and shorting a fresh gap-down is the same mistake I am here to unwind. Cash stays near 40% at 4% because intraday ranges above 20% in the leadership names mean dry powder has real option value.
novelty: This Round-3 book shares zero tickers and zero same-direction gross weight with Round 2: it is a concentrated semiconductor and enterprise-software relative-strength bet (SMH/SNOW/PANW long against two idiosyncratic single-name laggard shorts in ORCL and HOOD), whereas Round 2 is a diversified equal-weight, small-cap, industrial and energy breadth basket carrying a megacap-index short — and where the two touch the same exposure at all, they touch it in opposite directions, since Round 3 is long the semiconductor complex that sits inside the Nasdaq index Round 2 is short.
research_notes: Checked the two sessions that post-date the 7/30 decision (my book only filled at the 7/31 close). (1) Tape: 7/31 S&P +0.7% to 7,489.72, Nasdaq +1% to 25,373.85, Dow +276.97 to 52,485.03 — a fourth straight winning month. (2) The decisive item: Microsoft beat on Azure and rallied ~16% on 7/30; Amazon beat on cloud and rose 15.3% on 7/31; the four hyperscalers guided 2026 capex to a combined $720-745B — RAISED, not cut. (3) Semis inverted violently: SOXX +8%, Lam +17%, Micron +18% (then to ~$903 with a $744-911 intraday range), SanDisk +22%, WDC +18%, Seagate +16%, SK Hynix and Samsung +20% each, Korea's KOSPI +18%; Samsung warned the memory CRUNCH (shortage) extends into 2028. SMH closed $537.72 (52wk $279.19-$671.83), SOXL $115.63 (+0.79% on 7/31, i.e. flat after Thursday's rip). SOXQ +99% YTD. (4) Macro unchanged and reinforcing my Round-2 tilt: Fed held at 3.50-3.75% with three regional presidents (Hammack, Kashkari, Logan) dissenting for a HIKE — first unified three-way dissent since 2016; 30-year yield 5.22%, highest since 2007; Brent above $88 and +20% for July on renewed US-Iran fighting, with rising oil explicitly cited as the day's inflation worry. (5) Breadth intact: IWM $292.59, ~3% off its 52-week high, +31% y/y, +18.75% YTD. (6) Apple -7% to -9.5% on weak guidance, Services and China miss. (7) Oracle: down ~64% in 10 months, ~$130B debt, ~300% debt/equity, capex to ~$95B in FY27 and a planned $40B raise against a $638B backlog. (8) Mizuho channel checks favorable for SNOW/PANW/CRWD into earnings.
